notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2024, as the county reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by independent school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Payments to other governments ($53,748,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.
Political money is not scored: contributions to Texas county candidates were not loaded.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended July 31, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by independent school districts with their own taxes, so they are not included. Residents also pay Nueces County.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
Debt service leaves out $2,227,000 of principal repaid with new borrowing the city did not spend on capital that year, most likely refinancing or a rolled-over note.
Payments to other governments ($12,277,000) are left out, because the government receiving them reports that spending.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.
Political money is not scored: contributions to Texas city candidates were not loaded.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Cameras: 55 license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Corpus Christi's borders in OpenStreetMap (33 made by Flock Safety), not counting cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies. Flock cameras count as a red flag whoever runs them. Other brands count only when the government is the recorded operator, since many have no operator recorded.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Texas yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Flock camera network
redFlags.detail: 33 Flock Safety license-plate cameras are mapped inside City of Corpus Christi's borders in OpenStreetMap. Flock cameras photograph every passing car and feed a search network shared with police agencies across the country. Who runs each camera is not recorded; cameras tagged as run by stores, malls, schools or state and regional agencies are not counted.

source.label: OpenStreetMap license-plate cameras (as mapped by DeFlock)

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Corpus Christi Police Department operates two DJI drones as of 2014, according to data compiled by the Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College.
